\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related-work}

\paragraph{Formal reasoning with LLMs.}
LLM-solver pipelines~\citep{satlm, logic-lm, linc, fover-pei2025, lorp} and RL methods trained on solver feedback~\citep{polu2020generative, zelikman2022star, mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl, deepseek-prover-v15, deepseek-prover-v2, deepseek-r1-2025} evaluate execution accuracy alone, with no diagnostic for structural quality.
We use FOLIO~\citep{folio}, the only public NLI benchmark with both FOL and Prolog annotations.

\paragraph{Process rewards and reward shaping.}
Learned verifiers and PRMs~\citep{cobbe2021training, lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} provide step-level feedback but suffer from reward-model noise and distribution shift~\citep{processbench}; recent work extends PRMs to multi-domain settings~\citep{zeng2025versaprm} and process-level reasoning~\citep{khalifa2025thinkprm}. \citet{uesato2022solving} and \citet{gao-effective-rl-reward} show that auxiliary process/outcome rewards can \emph{hurt} RL training relative to success-only reward, a finding our ISR-as-reward results corroborate.
Unlike potential-based reward shaping~\citep{ng1999policy}, ISR augmentation does not preserve optimal policy, as it rewards output properties (component necessity) rather than state transitions, explaining the observed Goodhart vulnerability.
Symbolic feedback approaches~\citep{rlsf} use solver certificates as token-level rewards, achieving gains on program synthesis; ISR differs in operating at the component level (LOO ablation) rather than the token level, and our results show this structural signal is gamed when optimized.
Concurrent work by \citet{cao2026pushing} uses interleaved formal-logic verification bonuses during training (7B/14B models), dynamically penalizing intermediate fallacies; their verification-as-bonus approach faces similar Goodhart risks, though interleaving may mitigate the tautological collapse we observe under post-hoc ISR reward.
Rubric-grounded GRPO~\citep{rubric-grpo} uses structured LLM-judge rewards to improve generalization; ISR is solver-derived and deterministic rather than judge-based, but both represent structured alternatives to scalar execution reward.
The shared lesson across these approaches is that reward augmentation introduces proxy risk; our contribution is providing an empirical instance of this variant in the solver-backed RL setting, where the diagnostic itself becomes the optimization target.

\paragraph{Reward hacking and Goodhart's Law.}
Goodhart's Law~\citep{goodhart-1975} is established theoretically~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, skalse-reward-hacking, karwowski-goodhart-rl, everitt2021reward} and empirically across domains: RLHF and frontier models~\citep{amodei2016concrete, krakovna2020specification, gao-reward-overoptimization, bondarenko-spec-gaming, kim-game-formalization}, RL for text generation~\citep{paulus2018deep}, and goal misgeneralization in deep RL~\citep{langosco2022goal}.
\citet{kwa-catastrophic-goodhart} show that heavy-tailed reward misspecification causes \emph{catastrophic} Goodhart where KL regularization provably fails, offering a theoretical lens for why GRPO's KL penalty does not prevent the ISR collapse we observe.
Recent work further documents spurious reward signals in RLVR~\citep{spurious-rewards} and reward hacking in frontier models~\citep{metr-reward-hacking}.
\citet{wang2025trace} propose TRACE, which detects implicit reward hacking by measuring reasoning effort (truncated chain-of-thought AUC); STA/ISR measures structural necessity (component ablation) rather than effort, providing a complementary diagnostic axis.
Our setting differs in three ways: ISR is deterministic and solver-derived rather than learned; gaming \emph{emerges during RL training} rather than at inference time (cf.\ shortcut learning in supervised settings~\citep{geirhos2020shortcut}); and the effect operates at a diagnostic level, where the metric designed to detect gaming becomes gamed when optimized.
\citet{kim-game-formalization} document gaming at inference time on fixed models; our work extends this to training-time emergence, where GRPO's exploration-exploitation dynamics discover and amplify exploits that inference-time evaluation would not predict.
\citet{pan-reward-misspecification} show that more capable agents exploit reward misspecifications more severely; our cross-scale comparison (4B vs.\ 1.7B) complements this finding by demonstrating that different capacities discover qualitatively different exploits under identical reward formulations.
We frame our results as an empirical instance (primarily regressional, with extremal elements) of Goodhart's Law within the \citet{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} taxonomy: ISR's LOO definition creates an inherent structural bias toward tautology (single-premise-equals-conclusion receives $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$ by construction), with collapse observed at all four tested doses.

\paragraph{Mutation testing.}
STA adapts the LOO mutation paradigm~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey} to solver inputs; our contribution lies in the application and empirical findings, not in the perturbation primitive itself.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

STA exposes structural degeneration invisible to execution-based evaluation (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}), and ISR exhibits Goodhart collapse at all four tested doses (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}--\ref{sec:crossscale}).
At 500 steps, ISR produces descriptively more non-hacking output than random controls (Table~\ref{tab:goodhart-landscape}), but seed-level permutation tests are underpowered ($n{=}5$, $p{=}0.26$), the advantage reverses under stricter classification, and extended training confirms the window closes.
Snapshot evaluation at 500 steps would overestimate ISR's benefit; only trajectory analysis reveals the transient nature of any improvement.
The core asymmetry is clear: the same LOO structure that makes ISR a useful diagnostic also makes it a vulnerable optimization target, because tautological constructions satisfy component necessity by definition.
While Goodhart collapse under LOO-based metrics is theoretically predictable, the specific dynamics resist prediction from the metric definition alone: seed-dependent divergence, dose-varying collapse patterns, and cross-logic mode divergence each required empirical observation to identify.

All experiments use a single model family (Qwen3-4B/1.7B), one dataset (FOLIO), and one RL algorithm (GRPO).
The specific hacking modes and their relative prevalence may differ under other architectures or formal reasoning benchmarks, but the structural vulnerability of LOO-based metrics to tautological exploits follows from the metric definition and should transfer to any setting where the optimizer can reduce component count.
Our results illustrate a concrete instance of Goodhart's law in RL for formal reasoning~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}: the failure mode is regressional rather than extremal, with the optimizer concentrating probability mass on regions where ISR's structural bias coincides with degenerate outputs.
For scalable oversight of solver-backed systems, structural diagnostics should remain decoupled from the training loop.

The STA protocol (LOO ablation on solver inputs) applies beyond FOL and Prolog to any setting with a compositional input format and a binary verifier, including SMT solvers, proof assistants, and program synthesis with test suites.
TRACE~\citep{wang2025trace}, which detects reward hacking by measuring reasoning effort, provides a complementary diagnostic axis; combining structural necessity (STA) with effort-based detection (TRACE) may yield more robust hacking identification than either alone.
For practitioners, we recommend using ISR for post-hoc evaluation rather than as a training signal, reporting mode-level breakdowns alongside aggregate metrics, and evaluating across multiple seeds and training horizons to avoid overestimating structural quality from snapshot evaluations.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Experiments use a single model family (Qwen3-4B/1.7B), a single structured-NLI dataset (FOLIO, 500 training examples and 100 evaluation examples), and a single RL algorithm (GRPO).
Whether the specific hacking modes and collapse dynamics generalize to other architectures or larger-scale formal reasoning benchmarks remains open.
Our 1.7B experiments use three seeds per condition; strict non-hacking rates range from $0$--$3.7\%$ (ISR $\beta{=}0.1$) to $0$--$29\%$ (ISR $\beta{=}0.3$, driven by a single low-PR seed), and $N{=}3$ may miss rare non-hacking-capable initializations.
The automated classifier does not detect H9 (ex falso) at 1.7B; manual audit found H9 instances within taxonomy-classified categories, so 1.7B non-hacking rates may overestimate true rates.

ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity, not semantic faithfulness: a high-ISR proof can still be logically vacuous if its individually necessary premises are collectively inconsistent or semantically ungrounded.
A downstream NLI evaluation confirms this gap ($\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$; Appendix~\ref{app:extended-discussion}).
The current decomposition treats conclusion sub-expressions (quantifier, antecedent, consequent) as separate components; for tautological formulas where sub-expressions overlap with premises, ISR values can depend on decomposition granularity rather than proof structure, though these edge cases do not affect aggregate statistics.
Non-hacking is a residual classification: undiscovered gaming modes would reduce the true rate, as illustrated by H7b (obfuscated tautology evading text-match classifiers) and query-as-fact gaming in Prolog.
STA requires solvers supporting component-level input manipulation, adding $O(n)$ solver calls per sample (mean $n{\approx}6$--$8$ in our experiments, ${\sim}6$--$8{\times}$ evaluation overhead); at training time with ISR reward, this overhead applies to all proved rollouts per GRPO step.

Five seeds demonstrate qualitative divergence but limit statistical power for seed-level permutation tests ($p{\geq}0.26$; minimum achievable $p{=}0.008$ at $n{=}5$).
CMH tests yield $p{<}10^{-9}$ but assume within-stratum independence, which is violated when samples share a checkpoint and decoding strategy; CMH $p$-values should be interpreted as directional indicators, not calibrated significance levels.
Dose coverage is sparse: ISR $\beta{=}0.05$ and $\beta{=}0.2$ each use three seeds, the primary $\beta{=}0.1$ comparison uses five, and qualitative differences across doses should be treated as preliminary observations.
ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ s43 and s44 checkpoints were lost during disk cleanup, preventing retrospective H8 audit; the reported 5-seed pooled non-hacking rate (23\%) is an uncorrected upper bound.
We report individual $p$-values without correction for multiple comparisons; given the exploratory nature and limited seed counts, reported $p$-values are descriptive rather than confirmatory.
All 500-step results are temporal snapshots: trajectory analysis (1000 steps) confirms that the non-hacking window under ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ is transient (s42: $17\%{\to}2\%$; s45: $55\%{\to}0\%$), and 500-step non-hacking rates should be interpreted as upper bounds on long-run structural quality.
Whether SFT would exhibit hacking at higher prove rates (e.g., via best-of-$N$ sampling or scaled training data) remains an open question central to the RL-specificity claim.

1	\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	STA exposes structural degeneration invisible to execution-based evaluation, and ISR exhibits Goodhart collapse at all four tested doses.
5	The core asymmetry is that the same LOO structure making ISR a useful diagnostic also makes it a vulnerable optimization target: tautological constructions satisfy component necessity by definition.
6	Any transient non-hacking window at 500 steps ($p{=}0.26$, underpowered) reverses under stricter classification and disappears under extended training; snapshot evaluation overestimates ISR's benefit.
7	While collapse under LOO-based metrics is theoretically predictable, the specific dynamics (seed-dependent divergence, dose-varying patterns, cross-logic mode diversity) required empirical observation.
8	
9	All experiments use Qwen3 (4B/1.7B), FOLIO, and GRPO; hacking modes may differ under other architectures, but the structural vulnerability to tautological exploits follows from the LOO definition and should transfer to any setting where the optimizer can reduce component count.
10	Our results illustrate regressional Goodhart~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} in solver-backed RL: structural diagnostics should remain decoupled from the training loop.
11	STA applies to any compositional-input/binary-verifier setting (SMT solvers, proof assistants, program synthesis); combining it with effort-based detection~\citep{wang2025trace} may yield more robust hacking identification.

1	\section{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}

4	Experiments use a single model family (Qwen3-4B/1.7B), one dataset (FOLIO, 500 train / 100 eval examples), and one RL algorithm (GRPO); generalization of specific hacking modes to other architectures or benchmarks remains open.

711	\paragraph{ISR signal vs.\ training dynamics.}
712	At the \emph{ISR signal level}, the $O(1)$ variant is indistinguishable from exec-only: both produce near-zero ISR because models emit redundant premise copies whose individual removal never changes the proof outcome.

714	This confound depresses prove rate by 30 percentage points ($63\%$ vs.\ $93\%$ exec-only), making it impossible to attribute the difference purely to the ISR signal.
715	The result confirms that the $O(n)$ per-clause ablation is necessary for ISR to carry a structural signal, while also showing that even a minimal tautology guard alters training dynamics substantially.
